answer: The phrase has been used for different things. The PLO's 1968 charter claimed all of Mandatory Palestine, and Hamas's 2017 document uses the phrase in a sentence rejecting any alternative to liberating all of Palestine. Israel's Likud platform of 1977 claimed the same land for Israel alone. Some who use it today, such as a US congresswoman and 65 Northwestern student groups, say they mean freedom, human rights and coexistence. Jewish organisations say it calls for the end of Israel, and in April 2024 the US House called it 'outrightly antisemitic'. The Meta Oversight Board found that it has many meanings. Our reading: a parent should ask the speaker what they mean, and should know that in the Hamas, Likud and 1968 PLO documents cited here, the land is claimed for one side.

could_not_verify: The Likud platform's own Hebrew text and Likud's archive; the English wording comes from the Jewish Virtual Library and is confirmed by a 1977 JTA summary, the Oversight Board and Responsible Statecraft.
The first use of the phrase: sources put it in the mid-1960s PLO or in 1967-69; none gives a dated first use. AJC says its origins are unknown.

A US court or a US university ruling on the slogan: none found readable. The Berlin, Mannheim and Duesseldorf courts and the Meta Oversight Board are cited instead; only Harvard's president is cited from a university, as a statement and not a ruling.
ADL's own page on the slogan could not be loaded; ABC News and the AJC page are used for the Jewish-organisation reading. Hillel's national statements were not read.
The wording of the Berlin court's written reasons: only reports about it (LTO, JNS) were read.

Who translated the English texts. The Avalon pages for the 1968 PLO charter and the 1988 Hamas Covenant, Middle East Eye's 2017 Hamas document and the Jewish Virtual Library's Likud platform do not say who translated them; none is an official or agreed translation, and readings of single words (for example the date in Article 6 of the charter) are disputed. The Jewish Virtual Library is an advocacy publisher and is labelled so.

That the PLO later recognised Israel (1993) and its National Council voted in 1996 to cancel the charter articles that contradict that recognition: not on this card, so the 1968 charter is shown without its later revision.
The next sentence of Hamas's 2017 article 20, which treats a state on the 1967 lines as 'a formula of national consensus', is on the card era7-hamas-in-its-own-words and not here.
not_claimed: This card does not say the slogan is antisemitic, or that it is not. It records what the documents say and what each side says it means.
It does not say that everyone who chants the slogan wants Israel gone, or that none do.
It does not defend Hamas's document, the PLO's 1968 charter, or the Likud platform; it quotes them.
It does not say Likud's 1977 line and Hamas's line are morally the same; it says both claimed the same land for one side.

answer_claims.says: The phrase has been used for different things.
The PLO's 1968 charter claimed all of Mandatory Palestine, and Hamas's 2017 document uses the phrase in a sentence rejecting any alternative to liberating all of Palestine.
Israel's Likud platform of 1977 claimed the same land for Israel alone.
Some who use it today, such as a US congresswoman and 65 Northwestern student groups, say they mean freedom, human rights and coexistence.
Jewish organisations say it calls for the end of Israel, and in April 2024 the US House called it 'outrightly antisemitic'.
The Meta Oversight Board found that it has many meanings.
Our reading: a parent should ask the speaker what they mean, and should know that in the Hamas, Likud and 1968 PLO documents cited here, the land is claimed for one side.

skeptic.notes: Round 1. Read two or more sources per fact; every quote is on its page. Strongest objection from the chanting side: the 1968 charter is shown without its later revision (PLO recognition of Israel 1993, charter articles cancelled 1996); the 1969 'democratic state' line is there but the card is silent on the revision (should-fix, needs a new source). From the Jewish side: Hamas's 2017 sentence is quoted without the next sentence (a 1967-lines state, 'formula of national consensus'), which cuts both ways (should-fix); fact 2 would be fairer with it. Found and fixed: fact 5 said 'some universities' but only Harvard's president is cited (now narrowed); fact 4 said 'people' and 'equality' but its sources are one Tlaib tweet (NBC, Axios, Michigan Advance report the same tweet: one voice, not three) and one student letter that does not say 'equality' (narrowed to those two speakers). Must-fix for the writer: none blocks the facts as now worded. Translations: Avalon's charter, Middle East Eye's Hamas text and the Jewish Virtual Library's Likud text name no translator; recorded in could_not_verify. JVL is advocacy (already labelled). Responsible Statecraft is a think-tank magazine, labelled news; borderline, left. Oversight Board is 'primary' only for its own ruling; its Likud and Hamas lines are its description, corroborated by JTA and the Hamas text. H.Res. 883 is cited as introduced; the passed text was not read (should-fix). Axios returns 403 to the checker (archive copy used). Quotes: verified online below. Status stays draft until the revision of the charter and the 1967 sentence are added with sources.

citer.notes: Split the answer into seven sentences, each tied to facts. Removed: 'Both halves are true, because...' (the 'halves' were never defined and no fact says either half is true); 'Jewish organisations and the US House say it calls for the end of Israel' (fact 6 carries 'outrightly antisemitic', not 'end of Israel': reworded); 'Many people who chant it' (facts carry named speakers only: now 'Some ... such as'); 'where the phrase appears in official documents' (the PLO charter and Likud platform do not contain the phrase: now names the three documents). Every remaining sentence rests on the cited facts.
